<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, this project is an implementation of an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server tailored to work with the Notion API. It acts as a middleware to convert and process high-level instructions (like “Comment 'Hello MCP' on page 'Getting started'”) into the necessary API calls for the Notion API. Here’s how you can draw an accurate and detailed system design diagram of the project’s architecture:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   - Entry Points & Server Initialization:
     • scripts/start-server.ts and src/init-server.ts serve as the launch points for the server.
   - Core Server Functionality (inside src/openapi-mcp-server):
     • auth Module: Contains authentication logic. Include its index file, template, and type definitions.
     • client Module: Responsible for handling HTTP client operations – note that it includes tests for integration.
     • mcp Module: Implements the MCP protocol aspects (e.g., proxying requests), with components like the proxy.ts.
     • openapi Module: Contains functionality to parse and handle OpenAPI specifications and file uploads.
   - Supporting Files:
     • Build scripts, configuration (e.g., package.json, tsconfig.json), and test suites provide context but are not part of runtime architecture.
   - External Dependencies:
     • Notion API: While not hosted in the project, integration details in the README indicate how the MCP server acts on behalf of this external service.
     • Environment variables as configured (e.g., OPENAPI_MCP_HEADERS).

2. Relationships & Data Flow:
   - The “start-server” script (entry point) initializes the server, hooking together the MCP, auth, client, and openapi modules.
   - The auth module likely intercepts or processes requests that require authentication, using defined templates and types.
   - The client module handles outgoing HTTP calls (e.g., communication with Notion or other APIs) and coordinates with the mcp and openapi modules.
   - The mcp module acts as a mediator that maps high-level instructions into the appropriate series of API calls. For example, it might take a command like adding a page and direct that into API calls such as "v1/search" and "v1/comments".
   - The openapi module plays a critical role in parsing and dealing with OpenAPI specifications, ensuring proper file upload handling and overall compliance with the protocol.

3. Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
   - Modular Design: The code is partitioned into function-specific sub-modules (auth, client, mcp, openapi). This modular division is ideal for isolating responsibilities.
   - Layered Communication: Input from an API request goes through the initialization layer, then through authentication and protocol conversion layers before reaching the client that interacts with Notion.
   - Test-Driven: Presence of tests in each module indicates that the design is strongly oriented to verification at each layer.

4. Technologies & Frameworks:
   - Node.js with TypeScript is the main technology, as indicated by .ts files and tsconfig.json.
   - Notion API integration is central to the project.
   - npm is used for package management and build automation.

5. Tailoring the Diagram:
   - Begin by drawing a box labeled “Notion MCP Server” to encompass the whole system.
   - Inside this box, create sub-boxes for:
     • Server Initialization (scripts/start-server.ts, src/init-server.ts).
     • Authentication Module (auth folder: index.ts, template.ts, types.ts).
     • MCP Processing Module (mcp folder: proxy.ts, tests).
     • HTTP Client Service (client folder: http-client.ts + tests).
     • OpenAPI Handling Module (openapi folder: parser.ts, file-upload.ts, tests).
   - Outside the main server box, depict the external Notion API as an external system. Draw directional arrows from the HTTP Client Service module to the Notion API illustration showing the flow of requests/responses.
   - Optionally, illustrate environment configuration (from the README’s usage instructions) as a configuration source feeding into the server initialization.

6. Diagram Guidelines:
   - Ensure each component is clearly labeled using its module name (Auth, MCP, Client, OpenAPI).
   - Use directional arrows to indicate data flow:
     • Arrows from the start/initialization to each subsequent sub-module.
     • Arrows from the MCP processing module to the client module and from there to the Notion API.
   - Use color coding or distinct shapes: for example, use rectangular blocks for modules, ellipses for entry points, and cloud shapes for external systems.
   - Optionally include annotations noting the specific responsibilities of each module (e.g., “Auth: Handles request authentication”, “OpenAPI: Parses and validates API specs”, etc.).

7. Final Advice:
   - Focus on clarity and comprehensiveness – break down the project into the smallest logical components corresponding to actual directories/files.
   - While high-level connections suffice, ensure you also incorporate any relevant lower-level interactions (like parsing of multipart forms in the openapi module) if they significantly alter the data flow.
   - Make sure the diagram is self-contained: any software engineer reading it can understand how instructions flow from initial input to final API integration with Notion.

This detailed breakdown should help you (the principal software engineer) create a system design diagram that captures all essential components and interactions in the Notion MCP Server project in a clear, organized, and accurate manner.
</explanation>
